subsystems.name: Cell source
subsystems.role: supplies the living building blocks, ideally the patient's own so the implant is not rejected.

subsystems.name: Bio-ink
subsystems.role: carries cells through the printer and then holds them in place while they settle.
parts: hydrogel base (gelatin, alginate, collagen, hyaluronic acid)

subsystems.name: Printer
subsystems.role: deposits ink in the shape of the organ.
parts: print head (extrusion, inkjet, laser or light-based)

subsystems.name: Support and vasculature structure
subsystems.role: keeps hollow spaces open and leaves channels for blood once implanted.

subsystems.name: Bioreactor
subsystems.role: matures the printed construct from a fragile gel into tissue.

subsystems.name: Quality control
subsystems.role: proves the construct is sterile, alive and the right shape before it goes near a patient.

subsystems.name: Surgical delivery
subsystems.role: connects the organ to the patient's blood supply and drainage.

buildSteps.title: Take and grow the cells
buildSteps.detail: A small biopsy is taken from the patient, and the cells are either expanded directly or reprogrammed into stem cells that can become any of the organ's cell types, then multiplied in cleanroom culture.

buildSteps.title: Formulate the bio-ink
buildSteps.detail: Cells are mixed into a soft hydrogel at a density and viscosity the printer can push through a nozzle without shearing them apart.

buildSteps.title: Map the organ
buildSteps.detail: Medical imaging (CT or MRI) of the patient gives the dimensions the print must match, including where the vessels and ducts enter.

buildSteps.title: Print layer by layer
buildSteps.detail: The printer lays down cell-laden ink alongside a sacrificial ink that will later be washed out, building up the organ's shape. Different cell types are placed in their correct zones.

buildSteps.title: Set and clear the scaffold
buildSteps.detail: The hydrogel is gelled by light, temperature or ions, and the sacrificial ink is dissolved away to leave open, perfusable channels.

buildSteps.title: Mature in a bioreactor
buildSteps.detail: Over days to weeks the construct is perfused with oxygenated medium so cells survive, organise and secrete their own matrix. Thicker parts still starve because oxygen only diffuses about a tenth to a fifth of a millimetre.

buildSteps.title: Test the construct
buildSteps.detail: The team checks sterility, cell viability and that the printed geometry matches the plan.

buildSteps.title: Implant and connect
buildSteps.detail: The organ is surgically implanted and its vessels and ducts joined to the patient's. It must then grow its own capillary supply fast enough to stay alive.

prerequisites.why: an organ needs billions of cells, all grown to clinical purity.

prerequisites.tech: Bio-inks that set without killing cells
prerequisites.why: the printable gels used so far are too soft to hold a large organ's shape.
without vessels finer than about a tenth of a millimetre, the inside of a thick organ dies.
maturation takes weeks and must reach every cell.
each organ is a bespoke product made from one patient's cells, which existing approval paths handle awkwardly.

pathway.milestone: bioprinted tissues used for drug testing, plus simple flat and tubular implants in early human studies
pathway.unlocks: evidence that printed human cells survive and integrate.

pathway.milestone: blood vessels, bladder and airway patches made to order
pathway.unlocks: replacement parts that need no capillary bed of their own.

pathway.milestone: vascularised patches of heart or kidney tissue
pathway.unlocks: repair rather than replacement, on organs the patient still has.

pathway.milestone: whole solid organs with printed vessel trees
pathway.unlocks: an end to donor shortages — if perfusion, size and cost can all be solved.
